body_html:
A long distance relationship in Spanish runs on words: good-morning messages across time zones, late-night video calls, and a hundred ways of saying “I miss you”. If your partner speaks Spanish, writing to them in their language is one of the most meaningful things you can do, even if your Spanish isn’t perfect. In this guide I’ve collected the phrases couples actually use, from everyday texts to the words you’ll want on the day you finally see each other again.

Key takeaways
  • “I miss you” is te extraño (Latin America) or te echo de menos (Spain).
  • Short daily messages matter more than long letters.
  • Use terms of endearment naturally: mi amor, cariño, mi vida.
  • Counting down together builds excitement: ¡Quedan 10 días!
{{toc}}

How to say “I miss you” in Spanish

SpanishEnglishNotes
Te echo de menos.I miss you.Spain
Te extraño.I miss you.Latin America (understood everywhere)
Te echo muchísimo de menos.I miss you so much.Intensified
Me haces mucha falta.I really need you here.Deep, emotional
Ojalá estuvieras aquí.I wish you were here.Subjunctive
Cuento los días para verte.I’m counting the days until I see you.Romantic

The RAE dictionary lists echar de menos as a fixed expression meaning to miss someone or something. Spelling tip: it’s echo, without an h. See {{link:hecho-vs-echo|hecho vs echo}}.

Daily check-ins across the distance

For many more texts like these, see {{link:good-morning-messages-in-spanish|good morning messages in Spanish}} and {{link:good-night-messages-in-spanish|good night messages in Spanish}}.

Morning

  • ¡Buenos días, mi amor! ¿Has dormido bien? Good morning, my love! Did you sleep well?
  • Lo primero que hago al despertar es pensar en ti. The first thing I do when I wake up is think of you.
  • Que tengas un día precioso. Have a beautiful day.

Night

  • Buenas noches, cariño. Que descanses. Good night, darling. Sleep well.
  • Sueña conmigo. Dream of me.
  • Ojalá pudiera darte un beso de buenas noches. I wish I could kiss you good night.

Long distance relationship in Spanish: time zones and daily life

  • Aquí son las diez, ¿y allí? It’s ten here, what time is it there?
  • Cuando yo me acuesto, tú te levantas. When I go to bed, you’re getting up.
  • Cuéntame cómo te ha ido el día. Tell me how your day went.
  • Te mando una foto de mi desayuno. I’m sending you a photo of my breakfast.
{{image:2}}

Video call phrases

  • ¿Me oyes? Se ha congelado la imagen. Can you hear me? The picture froze.
  • Se corta. Te llamo otra vez. It’s cutting out. I’ll call you again.
  • ¡Qué guapa estás hoy! You look beautiful today!
  • No quiero colgar. I don’t want to hang up.
  • Cuelga tú. —No, tú. You hang up. —No, you.

More practical phone vocabulary in {{link:phone-calls-in-spanish|phone calls in Spanish}}.

Reassurance and commitment

  • La distancia no cambia lo que siento. Distance doesn’t change how I feel.
  • Merece la pena esperar por ti. You’re worth waiting for.
  • Pronto estaremos juntos. We’ll be together soon.
  • Estoy aquí para ti, aunque esté lejos. I’m here for you, even if I’m far away.
{{book:love-slowly}}

Counting down and planning visits

  • ¡Ya tengo los boletos! I’ve got the tickets! (billetes in Spain)
  • Quedan 15 días. Fifteen days to go.
  • ¿Qué quieres que hagamos cuando llegue? What do you want us to do when I arrive?
  • Te espero en el aeropuerto. I’ll wait for you at the airport.
  • ¡Por fin juntos! Together at last!

Terms of endearment

Spanish speakers sprinkle affectionate names through every message: mi amor, cariño, mi vida, cielo, corazón, mi rey / mi reina, and in Mexico mi cielo or bebé. Choose one or two that feel natural for you. The full list, with regional notes, is in {{link:spanish-terms-of-endearment|Spanish terms of endearment}}.

A sample message exchange

  • A: Buenos días, mi vida. Aquí está lloviendo y te echo de menos. (Good morning, my love. It’s raining here and I miss you.)
  • B: Buenas noches para mí, jaja. Yo también te extraño. ¿Hablamos luego por videollamada? (Good night for me, haha. I miss you too. Shall we video call later?)
  • A: ¡Claro! Y recuerda: quedan solo 12 días. (Of course! And remember: only 12 days left.)
  • B: Cuento cada uno. Te quiero. (I’m counting every one. I love you.)

Cultural notes

Many Spanish speakers express affection very openly in messages, with lots of emojis, besos and pet names, so don’t worry about sounding “too much”. Sign-offs like Un beso enorme, Besitos or Te quiero mucho are normal. Voice notes are hugely popular in Spanish-speaking countries; sending one, even a short Hola, mi amor, solo quería decirte que te echo de menos, can mean more than a long text. Families are often involved too, so learning a few phrases for your partner’s parents helps; see {{link:meeting-your-partners-family-in-spanish|meeting your partner’s family in Spanish}}.

Keeping the relationship strong

Phrases for the harder days matter too: Hoy ha sido un día difícil sin ti (Today was a hard day without you), Necesito oír tu voz (I need to hear your voice), Gracias por tu paciencia (Thank you for your patience). And small rituals help: a shared playlist (nuestra lista de canciones), watching the same movie at the same time (ver una peli a la vez), or reading the same book in two languages, one of the reasons I love bilingual books for couples.

Common mistakes

IncorrectCorrectWhy
Te pierdo.Te echo de menos / Te extraño.Perder = to lose
Te hecho de menos.Te echo de menos.From echar, no h
Ojalá estás aquí.Ojalá estuvieras aquí.Wish: imperfect subjunctive
Te amo on the third messageTe quiero early onTe amo is very strong

The difference between those last two is explained in {{link:te-quiero-vs-te-amo|te quiero vs te amo}}.

{{image:3}}

Final thoughts

Distance is hard, but words help. A simple Buenos días, te echo de menos every morning tells your partner they are on your mind, in their own language. For more everyday situations, see {{link:spanish-phrases-for-everyday-situations|my guide to Spanish phrases for everyday situations}}.

faq.q: How do you say “I miss you” in Spanish?
faq.a: Te extraño in Latin America, or te echo de menos in Spain. Both are understood everywhere.
